content.title: Habitat Trees in Arvada
content.summary: Habitat trees in Arvada are dead or dying trees that have been modified to provide shelter and food for wildlife, particularly birds. The city's forestry team assesses these trees for public safety and implements strategies to retain their habitat value, promoting biodiversity in urban areas. This initiative is part of a broader effort to mitigate habitat loss due to urbanization and support local ecosystems.
content.body:
## What is a Habitat Tree?

A habitat tree is a dead or dying tree that’s been modified and preserved to provide shelter, food, and nesting space for birds and other wildlife. Instead of removing the entire tree, the City's forestry team assess it for hazards and risk to the public. If hazards can be mitigated to reduce the risk presented to the public, then the tree is trimmed or modified in a way that mimics the natural decay seen in old-growth forests. These trees support biodiversity right in our neighborhoods.

Habitat trees are also sometimes called wildlife trees, snags, veteran trees, or special-use trees.

### Why It Matters

Birds and other cavity-dwelling animals play a vital role in urban ecosystems. They help with:

- Natural pest control
- Pollination and seed dispersal
- Waste decomposition
- Environmental monitoring (birds are indicators of ecological health)
- Inspiring community connection to nature and outdoor spaces

Unfortunately, Colorado’s rapid urbanization has caused significant habitat loss — especially for native and migratory birds. Since 1982, the state has lost more than 1,000 square miles of natural land to development. Habitat trees are one small but impactful way we can support birds and other species that rely on decaying wood and cavities in trees to survive.

## Arvada’s Approach

The City of Arvada's Habitat Tree initiative is based on a joint study from the City of Littleton in conjunction with CU Boulder designed for public implementation throughout the Front Range of Colorado.

The goal of the study — and Arvada’s initiative — is to promote safe, effective ways for cities to retain habitat value in trees slated for removal. Arvada is applying these science-based strategies to encourage healthier, more wildlife-friendly urban spaces for future generations.

- Read the full study: "[A Guide to Promote Bird Activity in Urban Environments through Hazardous Tree Mitigation](https://www.littletonco.gov/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/public-works/projects-docs-and-images/forestry/habitat/repurposing-hazard-for-habitat-on-the-colorado-front-range.pdf)"
- View the field guide: "[Repurposing Hazard Trees for Bird Habitat](https://www.littletonco.gov/files/sharedassets/public/v/1/public-works/projects-docs-and-images/forestry/habitat/repurposing-hazard-trees-for-bird-habitat-brochure.pdf)"

Not every dead tree qualifies as a habitat tree — public safety always comes first. Our forestry team begins by assessing the hazards present and the risk it poses to the public. If the risk presented by the hazard can appropriately be reduced, then a tree can be retained for habitat.

Types of habitat tree pruning you may see in our parks are:

- Low-risk snags may be left standing with minor pruning.
- Intermediate techniques like scoring, cornet cuts, or trunk wounding help mimic natural decay and support insect and bird activity.
- Advanced methods include carving artificial cavities or installing bird boxes designed for species like woodpeckers, nuthatches, or bluebirds.

These strategies align with habitat needs identified in the Littleton-CU Boulder study, including cavity size, height, and tree location preferences of common Front Range birds.
